stories.title: Big US banks curb AI agents after unauthorised account access
points: Axios reports that big US banks are finding third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, usually logged in with the customer’s own password, and some acting beyond instructions. Morgan Stanley is blocking them; JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi are restricting them; most banks lean towards read-only access.

In an FT column, John Thornhill argues firms must ‘Know Your Agent’: identify it, keep it behaving as intended and settle who is liable when it errs. He cites Deloitte: 74% of companies plan to use agents within two years.
404 Media shows ID checks already strain: a scammer opened a CashApp account in Amanda Smith’s name, and she was charged.
numbers: of firms plan to use AI agents within two years (Deloitte, via FT)
big US banks named as blocking or restricting agents
stories.why: Banks spent decades perfecting Know Your Customer. Agents break that model: the login is genuine, but the person may not be the one acting.
stories.other: Customers will want agents to pay bills and move money, and bankers admit a middle ground is needed. Blanket bans may only push password-sharing out of sight; vetted, read-only or signed agent access could prove safer.

stories.title: AI researchers leave OpenAI, DeepMind to build startups in India
points: Inc42 tracks researchers leaving global labs to build in India: Shyamal Anadkat, who led OpenAI’s Applied Evals team, founded Empirical Machines for AI-driven molecule and materials research; ex-DeepMind engineer Parth Sarthi’s Chariot builds speech-native models under the IndiaAI Mission.
Former Google engineering director Anish Das Sarma’s Reinforce Labs red-teams enterprise AI. Empirical Machines is reportedly in talks to raise about $15 Mn, per Moneycontrol.
Investors say lab pedigree helps recruit talent but does not prove a business; DeVC’s Rahul Mathur asks who will pay for the research.
numbers: YoY rise in Indian AI funding, Q3 2026 (Inc42)
raise Empirical Machines is reportedly in talks for
stories.why: The scarce input in AI is people who have trained frontier models. If even a few build here, India gains not just companies but the researchers they go on to train.
stories.other: Pedigree is not product. Research takes years to pay off, compute is costly, and investors say customers, not résumés, will decide which of these startups survive.
stories.imageAlt: KKReckons explainer, India's AI homecoming: Indian AI funding rose 235% year on year in Q3 2026 (Inc42). Ex-OpenAI, DeepMind and Google staff are building startups in India, helped by the IndiaAI Mission and peers like Sarvam AI.
stories.emailTeaser: Ex-OpenAI and DeepMind talent bets on building from India.
stories.cite: Indian AI startup funding rose 235% year on year in Q3 2026, according to an Inc42 report cited on 21 Oct 2026.

stories.title: AI stocks drove $138bn in gains for US public pensions, WSJ finds
points: A WSJ analysis of 13 large public pensions finds a basket of 15 AI-linked stocks drove $138 billion in paper gains from late 2022 to June, rising to about 27% of their US equity holdings.
Yet officials in the same states are slowing data centres: New York paused many new projects in July, and Pennsylvania’s governor tightened approval rules in August.
The Equable Institute says the boom has nearly restored pre-2008 funding levels; a sharp downturn could leave governments facing tens of billions in costs.
numbers: AI-linked paper gains, 13 funds, end-2022 to June
AI basket’s share of their US stocks
stories.why: Teachers and firefighters are quietly long the AI trade. Concentration risk now sits in retirement funds most beneficiaries never chose.
stories.other: Pensions mostly track indexes, so the AI weight reflects the market, not a bet. Selling to make a political point has cost retirees before, and trustees’ duty is to risk-adjusted returns.
stories.imageAlt: KKReckons explainer, Your pension is long AI: $138bn in AI-linked paper gains for 13 big US public pensions from end-2022 to June 2026. AI stocks are about 27% of their US shares, while New York and Pennsylvania push back on data centres.
stories.emailTeaser: Politicians fight data centres their pension funds profit from.
stories.cite: AI-linked stocks drove $138 billion in paper gains for 13 large US public pensions from end-2022 to June 2026, a WSJ analysis found.

stories.title: AI bull market is no dotcom bubble, argues Bloomberg’s Nir Kaissar
points: In a Bloomberg Opinion column carried by Mint, Nir Kaissar argues the AI rally lacks the euphoria that drives bubbles: bears now outnumber bulls by 8 percentage points in AAII surveys, while bulls led by over 20 points in the late 1990s.
He concedes AI’s grip is bigger: AI firms make up 40% to 60% of US market value and nearly 70% of S&P 500 third-quarter earnings growth, per Citadel Securities estimates.
His forecast: profit growth cools and a pullback follows, but absent a crisis, nothing worse than an ordinary bear market.
numbers: bears ahead of bulls, AAII survey
of S&P 500 Q3 earnings growth from AI firms (Citadel est.)
stories.why: Sentiment is a useful tell, but read it with today’s pensions story: when AI carries most of the market’s growth, even an ordinary bear market lands on retirees.
stories.other: Scepticism alone does not prevent a bust. Concentration is higher than in 1999, earnings can disappoint, and as Kaissar admits, bubbles are hard to call in real time.
stories.imageAlt: KKReckons explainer, Bubble? Too gloomy: bears lead bulls by 8 points in AAII surveys, against a 20-plus-point bull lead in the late 1990s. AI firms make up 40% to 60% of US market value, and profit growth is likely to cool.
stories.emailTeaser: Bears outnumber bulls by 8 points; a columnist says relax.
stories.cite: AI-related companies accounted for nearly 70% of S&P 500 earnings growth in Q3 2026, according to Citadel Securities estimates cited by Bloomberg Opinion.

stories.title: Private credit firms court retail investors with festivals and F1
points: The WSJ reports asset managers are courting wealth advisers at events like California’s Future Proof Festival, where nearly 6,000 attendees got concerts, wellness classes and private-credit pitches, as institutional clients reach their limits.
Carlyle uses a Red Bull F1 sponsorship; Blue Owl and EQT back tennis; Apollo sponsors a PGA golfer.
Withdrawals are rising: investors pulled an estimated $30 billion from retail-marketed funds in 2026’s first three quarters, per Robert A. Stanger, and many funds limit quarterly exits.
numbers: pulled from retail private-credit funds, Q1–Q3 2026 (Stanger)
attendees at the Future Proof Festival
stories.why: When a product needs a beach festival to sell, ask who carries the risk. Individual investors pay higher fees than pensions and cannot always get out quickly.
stories.other: Supporters say it opens returns once reserved for institutions, and advisers insist perks don’t sway their picks. For some clients a small allocation can make sense.
stories.imageAlt: KKReckons explainer, Loans, sold with a beach party: an estimated $30bn was withdrawn from retail-marketed private-credit funds in Q1 to Q3 2026 (Robert A. Stanger). Firms pitch with concerts, F1, tennis and golf, while many funds limit quarterly withdrawals.
stories.emailHead: Come for the concert, stay for credit
stories.emailTeaser: Concerts and F1 sell hard-to-exit loan funds to advisers.
stories.cite: Investors withdrew an estimated $30 billion from retail-marketed private-credit funds in the first three quarters of 2026, according to Robert A. Stanger.

stories.title: Family firm with no layoffs in 75 years becomes a model for bosses
points: The WSJ profiles Gund Co., a St. Louis composite-materials maker founded by the CEO’s grandfather that has never laid anyone off and has averaged 18% annual growth for a decade.
CEO Steve Gund’s people-first playbook: red cards on the factory floor flag problems, everyone has a development plan, financials are posted openly, and workers own part of the firm.
It is not soft: Gund staffs lean to ride out slow patches and manages out those who don’t adapt. Leaders from many companies have visited; few copy it fully.
numbers: average annual growth over a decade
stories.why: In a year of AI-driven job cuts, Gund argues keeping people can be a growth strategy, not a cost. Its secret is discipline as much as kindness.
stories.other: A private family firm answers to no quarterly investors and can staff lean by choice. What works on a Midwest factory floor may not survive a deep downturn, a sale or an industry remade by AI.
stories.imageAlt: KKReckons explainer, No layoffs in 75 years: Gund Co. has averaged 18% annual growth over the past decade. Every worker has a development plan and financials are posted openly; lean staffing and managing out non-adapters are the trade-offs.
stories.emailTeaser: Gund grows about 18% a year without a single layoff.
stories.cite: Gund Co. has averaged 18% annual growth for a decade without ever laying off an employee, the WSJ reported on 22 Oct 2026.

stories.title: Terence Tao calls for ‘Maths 2.0’ as AI floods the field with proofs
points: In a Nature World View column, Fields medallist Terence Tao says AI-aided proofs have appeared for hundreds of long-standing problems in recent months, and calls for a ‘Maths 2.0’ no longer defined by scarce proofs.

He flags costs: OpenAI’s 6 October release of hundreds of solutions disrupted research programmes; many AI results miss publication standards; credit for prior work is unclear; juniors lose a route to recognition.
He warns understanding lags output, ‘proof indigestion’, and sees similar risks in opaque models used for bank lending.
stories.why: When proofs become cheap, understanding becomes the scarce good. The same gap appears wherever banks and funds lean on models nobody can explain.
stories.other: Tao uses AI in his own research and says that, used creatively and with the right incentives, it could deepen understanding. The upheaval may be a transition cost, not a lasting loss.
stories.imageAlt: KKReckons explainer, Maths has proof indigestion: hundreds of long-standing problems got AI-aided proofs in recent months, Terence Tao says. Many AI results miss publication standards; Tao calls for new incentives and more responsible use of AI.
stories.emailTeaser: AI cracked hundreds of old problems; Tao says digestion lags.

stories.title: Warhound raises $200mn to clone and gene-edit US military dogs
points: The FT reports Warhound, conceived by Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey and Colossal Biosciences’ Ben Lamm, has raised $200mn from backers including Sequoia, Ark Invest and the CIA-founded In-Q-Tel to rebuild US supply of military working dogs.
It plans to clone top dogs and gene-edit them for longevity and performance; Anduril will develop body armour and ‘cybernetics’. Most such dogs now come from European breeders.
Luckey holds no equity and no daily role; ex-Pentagon data chief David Spirk will run it.
numbers: valuation including the new money, per a source
stories.why: Defence-tech money is now flowing into biology, not just drones. Who sets the ethical rules for editing animals for war is still an open question.
stories.other: Lamm argues editing is more humane, since many working dogs fail training today. But it is a promise, not a result: edited dogs still have to prove they outperform well-bred ones.
stories.imageAlt: KKReckons explainer, Better dogs, by design: Warhound raised $200mn to clone and gene-edit US working dogs, backed by Sequoia, Ark Invest, Lux Capital and In-Q-Tel. Anduril adds armour; ex-Pentagon data chief David Spirk leads.
stories.emailTeaser: Cloned, gene-edited working dogs draw $200mn from Sequoia and Ark.
stories.cite: Warhound raised $200mn from investors including Sequoia and Ark Invest, the FT reported on 22 Oct 2026.

takeaway.line: From bank logins to pensions and beach-tent fund pitches, one question runs through today: who is really making the call, and who holds the bill when it goes wrong?
